title: City air: cleaner in one place, dirtier in another
summary: Over the same 21 years (2005 to 2025), nitrogen dioxide from traffic and industry fell over Los Angeles and rose over fast-growing Dhaka.

finding.interpretation: The tropospheric NO2 column above Los Angeles declined by -0.163 × 10¹⁵ molecules cm⁻² per year (‑1.63 × 10¹⁵ molecules cm⁻² per decade) from 2005 to 2025, amounting to a -77.4 % change over the period, a statistically significant trend (p = 7.48e-20) that is consistent across all seasons and spatial cells. Seasonal analyses all show significant negative slopes, with the strongest winter (DJF) decline of -0.187 × 10¹⁵ molecules cm⁻² yr⁻¹. The effect size (≈7.1 × the inter‑annual variability) indicates the change is large relative to natural fluctuations, and the trend is robust according to the applied false‑discovery‑rate control.
finding.limitations: A documented change point in 2014 and the OMI row anomaly beginning in 2007 may introduce step‑like shifts that a monotonic trend cannot separate from gradual change, potentially biasing the magnitude of the reported decline. Consequently, while the trend is statistically robust, interpretation of its physical drivers requires caution.

provenance.processing_method: Monthly OMI Level 3 (Aura) values on 16 grid cells averaged over the region with cos(latitude) area weights (a month counts only when at least 70% of the region's area has data), the average seasonal cycle (monthly climatology over the record) subtracted to give anomalies, then trend-tested; annual means are shown for reference.

finding.interpretation: The tropospheric NO₂ column above Dhaka increased at an average rate of 0.089 × 10¹⁵ molecules cm⁻² yr⁻¹ (0.890 × 10¹⁵ molecules cm⁻² decade⁻¹), amounting to a 55.9 % rise (total change = 1.78 × 10¹⁵ molecules cm⁻²) over the 2005‑2025 period. This upward trend is statistically significant (p = 0.0106; 95 % CI 0.0316–0.1381) and is observed consistently across all 16 spatial cells, with each cell showing a significant positive slope. Seasonal analysis reveals significant increases in DJF, MAM, and JJA, while SON shows a non‑significant rise. The effect size (|total change|/σ ≈ 6.91) indicates that the observed change is large relative to natural inter‑annual variability, suggesting potential scientific relevance beyond mere statistical significance.
finding.limitations: The effective sample size is only about 6 due to strong lag‑1 autocorrelation (0.55), limiting the independence of observations. A documented change point in 2011 and the OMI row anomaly beginning in 2007 may contribute to the apparent trend, and the p‑value does not meet a stricter 0.01 threshold, warranting cautious interpretation.
